claim: TypeSafe's Score guidance says level descriptions should describe concrete situations rather than adjective degrees, and tells you to check the answers against known examples.
quote: Describe situations, not degrees. "Broken or degraded feature, but workaround exists" gives the model something to match the state against. "Moderately severe" doesn't. Concrete descriptions can help the model distinguish levels. Check the answers against known examples
why: Direct official answer to concrete-vs-adjective level wording

claim: Each Score level is judged on its own: the model never sees level numbers or neighbouring levels, so relative wording and numbers in level text add no signal.
quote: Every level is evaluated separately. The model doesn't see a level's number or its neighbours, so "worse than the previous level" means nothing to it, and numbers in the descriptions or the instructions don't help.
why: Rules out relative or numeric level labels such as '1-5' or 'stronger than above'

claim: Score criteria go in low-to-high order, with at least 2 and at most 10 levels; array position is the level number.
quote: `criteria`: An ordered array of level descriptions, from the low end of the scale to the high end. Should have at least two levels; the API accepts up to 10.

claim: Recommended level count is as many as can be described distinctly, up to 10; three is acceptable; each Score should measure one dimension only.
quote: Use as many levels as you can describe distinctly, up to 10. Three is fine. Don't add levels you can't describe distinctly. Keep each Score question to one dimension. If a description says "punctual and smart and experienced", the question is measuring three things
why: How many levels to use, plus the one-dimension rule for evidence-strength scoring

claim: When neighbouring levels get confused, TypeSafe recommends level objects with the same field names on every level (for example `what` plus `examples`); examples help only when they resemble real inputs (Safari report: confidence went from 0.35 to 0.96 with a matching example and stayed at 0.35 with an unrelated one).
quote: give each level an object instead of a string, with a field for what the level covers and a field with a few example situations. Use the same field names on every level so the model can compare like with like.
why: Escalation path for level wording, with measured effect

claim: For Choice, both option names and descriptions are sent to the model (question IDs are not), so descriptions should separate options from each other; `null` descriptions are fine for self-explanatory names.
quote: The model never sees the question id. The option names and their descriptions are both sent to the model, so write descriptions that separate the options from each other.
why: How to write option descriptions; option keys are model-visible

claim: TypeSafe recommends giving the full option list (up to 255) instead of a shortlist, and adding an `other` or `none of the above` option when the list might not cover every input.
quote: A Choice question accepts up to 255 options, and adding options costs a few tokens each, so give the model the full list ... Add an `other` or `none of the above` option when the list might not cover every input, so the model can say none of the others fit.

claim: For easily confused Choice options, TypeSafe shows object descriptions with self-chosen fields such as `what`, `not_for`, and `examples`; field names are free-form and the model sees them.
quote: When two options are similar and the model keeps confusing them, describe each one with an object instead of a string. Give it fields for what the option covers, what belongs to a neighboring option instead, and a few example inputs.

claim: Type selection: Choice for unordered known sets, Score for a describable spectrum, Noul for a clean yes/no where the probability is the signal; if two types fit, prefer the one your code can act on directly.
quote: Use Noul for a yes/no judgment and Score to measure a position on a spectrum. "Is this candidate strong in Python?" needs a clear definition of "strong". A Noul value of 0.5 means the model gives yes and no equal probability. It does not mean the candidate has a medium skill level.
why: Choice vs Score vs Noul decision rule; warns against using Noul for degree

claim: Noul wording rules: one condition per Noul, phrase it so a high value means yes, a statement works as well as a question, and make the yes/no boundary unambiguous; add true/false criteria only when the boundary is subtle, and test with and without them.
quote: The instruction is enough for most Nouls, so try your questions with and without `criteria` and keep whichever gives better answers on your documents.
why: Noul with or without criteria; polarity and single-condition rules

claim: Jev-1.13 reads instructions literally, so TypeSafe says to state the exact condition and put boundary cases in the criteria; misaligned criteria (for example Noul true mapped to 'no') perform worse.
quote: `jev-1.13` answers the question you wrote, not the one you meant. Scoping words, negations, and implied conditions are read at face value... state the exact condition in the `instructions`. Be specific. Put boundary cases in the criteria.
why: Official jaggedness doc on instruction wording

claim: The jev-1.13 jaggedness doc warns against negations or double negatives, multi-hop indirection, numeric/date/counting tasks, irrelevant state, and assuming Noul and its negation sum to 1 (measured 0.72 + 0.47 = 1.19).
quote: Instructions carrying double negatives or complex indirection are answered less reliably. A question about a property of a property or something that requires multiple hops of reasoning costs accuracy. **Instead:** write your instructions as directly as possible.
why: Do's and don'ts list; structural non-invariance between question types

claim: TypeSafe recommends batching every question about the same state in one request; questions are independent, and its GDPR cookbook found batching 13 questions gave the same answers as separate calls at 12.2x lower cost.
quote: Runs a 13-question regulatory briefing over the GDPR Wikipedia article, showing that batching every question into one TypeSafe call is 12.2x cheaper and 10.0x faster with no change in answers.
why: Batching guidance with evidence that answers are unchanged

claim: Instructions should be one snap judgment; complex judgments should be split into several questions and weighted in code (composite scoring).
quote: Ask for a judgment a knowledgeable person makes in a second given the right context. "Does this message convey urgency?" is a good question. "Analyze this message and determine the best course of action" is not.

claim: TypeSafe's official agent skill tells agents that Score levels must describe concrete situations, to include a no-match outcome, and to state speculative premises explicitly; the docs add that agents are not good at writing questions.
quote: Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand on their own. Keep the needed answers available. Include a no-match outcome when nothing may fit; use a separate presence judgment when it is independently useful.
why: Condensed official checklist, matches the docs

claim: A third-party LMS guide reports 73.3% agreement with human tags at a mean confidence of 0.849 in a criteria-wording test, and blames overlapping criteria for confidently wrong answers.
quote: Jev's tags agreed with human-assigned tags 73.3% of the time, with a mean confidence of 0.849... points at ambiguous or overlapping criteria wording as the more likely lever than the model itself.
why: Weak independent data point on criteria overlap; small n=15, not TypeSafe
